Oregon’s pioneering decriminalization effort is set to end on Sunday, when a new statute takes effect that once again makes possessing small quantities of hard drugs illegal. Under HB4002, individuals found with substances such as fentanyl, heroin or methamphetamine can opt either to face a possession charge or to enter a treatment pathway that involves completing a behavioral‑health program and joining a deflection initiative designed to keep them out of court. Simple possession would be classified as a misdemeanor carrying a possible jail term of up to six months.

***
The law’s goal is to give police clearer authority to act against drug use in public spaces and to impose tougher penalties for selling drugs near locations like parks. While the statute encourages counties to develop treatment alternatives that divert people from the criminal justice system toward addiction and mental‑health services, it does not require them to do so. Supporters argue this flexibility lets each county tailor solutions to its resources, whereas critics warn it could produce a confusing and uneven patchwork of rules across the state.

***
Portland police chief Bob Day explained that eligibility for the deflection option is limited: a person must have no other charges, no outstanding warrants, no violent behavior and be medically stable. When someone meets those criteria, officers contact the county’s deflection dispatch line to share basic information, verify eligibility and link the individual with a mobile behavioral‑health outreach team that has thirty minutes to make contact.

***
Day added that if the behavioral‑health responders cannot arrive within that half‑hour window, the officer will proceed with an arrest rather than wait. He emphasized that the department cannot afford to linger on scene when the prescribed time limit expires.
